flagged.title: Part 1: Silas's Exile & the Gold
flagged.reason: The video states that Eliot explicitly writes the coins had become his 'companions', which teaches an incorrect quotation and contradicts the corrected mark scheme and knowledge-check question for this lesson.

mark_affecting.quote: George Eliot explicitly writes that the coins had become his familiars, and his companions.

flagged.title: Character Analysis
flagged.reason: The video incorrectly attributes Godfrey Cass's famous quotation ('There's debts we can't pay like money debts') to Nancy Lammeter, which would lose marks for text and character knowledge on a GCSE English Literature exam.

mark_affecting.video_says: Nancy doesn't fly into some vindictive rage; she responds with this calm, steady dignity. You absolutely need to memorise this quote for your exams: 'There's debts we can't pay like money debts.' It's so powerful because it shows her deep acceptance of moral responsibility.
mark_affecting.lesson_says: Godfrey’s reply to her — “there’s debts we can’t pay like money debts” — is one of the novel’s most important statements.

flagged.title: Key Themes & Exam Technique
flagged.reason: The video incorrectly claims the Silas Marner question assesses AO4 for spelling, punctuation, and grammar across four objectives, which would cause students to fail lesson knowledge check questions.

mark_affecting.quote: Marking criteria: AO1 (texts), AO2 (language), AO3 (context), and AO4 (written expression).
